skill.name: broken-authentication-testing
skill.description: Guides authorized testing for broken authentication, session handling, password policies, MFA controls, and password reset workflows in web applications.

security_audit.summary: Most external-command detections are false positives caused by Markdown code fences, not executable backtick usage. Several network and blocker findings are confirmed because the skill provides actionable guidance for credential attacks, rate-limit evasion, MFA bypass, session fixation, and password reset account takeover testing. No prompt injection attempt was found in SKILL.md.

remediation.issue: Credential stuffing and brute-force procedures include operational attack steps.
remediation.suggestion: Replace attack workflows with defensive checklists, safe rate-limit validation, and lab-only test account procedures.

remediation.issue: Detection evasion guidance covers IP rotation, user-agent randomization, and bypass headers.
remediation.suggestion: Remove evasion tactics and focus on verifying that controls detect or block these attempts.

remediation.issue: MFA, session fixation, and password reset sections include account takeover workflows.
remediation.suggestion: Rewrite examples to describe expected secure behavior, evidence to collect, and remediation without victim or admin takeover steps.

remediation.issue: Copyable command and request examples can be run against real services.
remediation.suggestion: Use clearly labeled lab targets, non-routable examples, and explicit authorization gates before active testing steps.

content.value_statement: Authentication flaws can expose accounts, sessions, and reset workflows to takeover. This skill guides authorized testers through structured checks and reporting.
actual_capabilities: Maps common login, registration, reset, logout, API, and OAuth endpoints.
Reviews password policy controls and weak credential acceptance.
Checks username enumeration signals from messages, timing, and status codes.
Assesses session cookie flags, token randomness, timeout behavior, and logout invalidation.
Evaluates MFA enrollment, OTP handling, recovery flows, and bypass conditions.
Organizes findings into authentication reports with remediation guidance.
limitations: Requires written authorization and scoped test accounts before active testing.
Does not provide live scanning or verification without user-supplied target details.
May be limited by CAPTCHA, rate limits, MFA controls, and production safety rules.
Third-party identity providers may require separate approval and testing methods.

use_cases.title: Prelaunch Authentication Review
use_cases.description: Assess login, reset, and session controls before a web application release.

use_cases.title: Penetration Test Planning
use_cases.description: Build an authorized test plan for authentication and session management weaknesses.

use_cases.title: Remediation Verification
use_cases.description: Confirm that password policy, lockout, MFA, and reset fixes work as intended.

prompt_templates.title: Plan A Safe Assessment
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner planning for an authorized test.
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a scoped broken authentication test plan for my authorized application. Include prerequisites, test accounts, safety limits, and report sections.

prompt_templates.title: Review Password Controls
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me assess password policy and username enumeration risks for this login flow. Focus on observations, safe tests, and remediation.

prompt_templates.title: Evaluate Session Security
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze my session handling design for cookie flags, token rotation, idle timeout, absolute timeout, and logout invalidation gaps.

prompt_templates.title: Build An Auth Report
prompt_templates.prompt: Turn these authorized authentication test notes into a professional report with risk ratings, evidence summaries, impact, and remediation steps.

output_examples.input: Assess a login flow for username enumeration.
output: Finding: Login responses differ for valid and invalid usernames.
Impact: Attackers can identify real accounts before password attacks.
Remediation: Use a consistent response message and normalize timing.
Observation: The session cookie includes Secure and HttpOnly flags.
Gap: SameSite is missing, which may increase cross-site request risk.
Recommendation: Set SameSite to Lax or Strict based on product needs.
Risk area: Reset tokens must be random, short lived, single use, and account bound.
Evidence needed: Token lifetime, reuse behavior, and account binding checks.
Fix: Invalidate used tokens and reject cross-account reset attempts.

best_practices: Use only authorized targets, scoped test accounts, and approved testing windows.
Prefer defensive validation and evidence collection over aggressive automation.
Document impact, reproduction boundaries, and concrete remediation for each finding.
anti_patterns: Running credential attacks against production users or unapproved systems.
Testing with real breached credentials or accessing real user accounts.
Sharing bypass steps without context, authorization limits, and remediation.

faq.question: Is this skill only for authorized testing?
faq.answer: Yes. It should only be used with written authorization, scoped targets, and approved test accounts.

faq.question: Can it run tests automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides methodology and reporting guidance. The user controls any testing tools and target access.

faq.question: What authentication areas does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers password policies, username enumeration, brute-force defenses, sessions, MFA, and password reset workflows.

faq.question: Does it support Claude, Codex, and Claude Code?
faq.answer: Yes. The generated metadata lists Claude, Codex, and Claude Code as supported tools.

faq.question: What evidence should a tester collect?
faq.answer: Collect scoped requests, response differences, session behavior, timestamps, screenshots, and remediation notes.

faq.question: What are the main safety limits?
faq.answer: Do not test real users, real breached credentials, third-party providers, or production systems without explicit approval.
